title: Headache, bleeding gums and dark urine

source.citation: Sea JL, Gassner SF, Smart J. Case Report of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura in a Previously Healthy Adult. J Educ Teach Emerg Med. 2021;6(1):V1-V4.

presentation.hpi: Sharp, constant headache for 7 days, rated 6/10. For the past 2–3 days he has had fatigue, palpitations, pallor and bleeding gums. On questioning he reports that his urine has been dark for about a week. Previously healthy.
presentation.family: No family history of autoimmune disorders.

exam: Generalized skin pallor and conjunctival pallor
Dry, pale mucous membranes with dried gingival blood between the teeth
Dark reddish-brown urine passed in the ED
Neurologically intact apart from nonfocal weakness, with a slow but normal gait
4 h after arrival: new word-finding difficulty with preserved comprehension and repetition; otherwise neurologically intact

imaging.modality: CT head (repeated at the onset of word-finding difficulty)

diagnosis.primary: Immune-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (ADAMTS13 activity <5% with anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies)
differentials: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (Shiga toxin or complement-mediated)
Evans syndrome (autoimmune hemolysis with immune thrombocytopenia)
Severe vitamin B12 deficiency with pseudo-microangiopathy

management: Provisional diagnosis from the clinical picture and a PLASMIC score of 6; ICU admission; ADAMTS13 sent to an external laboratory
Therapeutic plasma exchange, red cell transfusion and corticosteroids started immediately, without waiting for the ADAMTS13 result
Rituximab on ICU day 3 because anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies persisted
In total 10 plasma exchanges, 5 units of red cells and 1 dose of rituximab; discharged on a prednisone taper with pantoprazole, with three further rituximab doses planned
outcome: Back to his neurological baseline the next day, with improving renal function; platelets normalized to 150,000/µL on day 6. Discharged on day 10 with stable hemoglobin and platelets off plasma exchange.
teachingPoints: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, reticulocytosis, negative DAT) with severe thrombocytopenia is TTP until proven otherwise.
Near-normal PT, aPTT and INR help separate TTP from DIC; severe thrombocytopenia with only mild kidney injury favors TTP over HUS.
ADAMTS13 results take days: a PLASMIC score of 6–7 supports starting plasma exchange and corticosteroids at once (ISTH 2020 TTP guidelines); delays beyond 24 h are linked to higher mortality.
Neurological signs in TTP fluctuate, and a normal CT does not exclude microvascular ischemia.
Platelet transfusion is generally avoided unless bleeding is life-threatening; rituximab and caplacizumab are adjuncts in immune TTP.

questions.extra: Hb 4.7 g/dL, platelets 10,000/µL, reticulocytes 18.7%, schistocytes on smear, LDH 1885 U/L, haptoglobin <30 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, DAT negative. PT 15.2 s, aPTT 30.2 s, INR 1.2; creatinine 1.4 mg/dL.
questions.explanation: DAT-negative hemolysis with schistocytes plus profound thrombocytopenia is a thrombotic microangiopathy, and neurological symptoms with only mild kidney injury point to TTP. Near-normal coagulation argues against DIC, the negative DAT against Evans syndrome, and mild kidney injury in an adult makes Shiga toxin HUS less likely.

questions.q: His PLASMIC score is 6. What does this mean for management?
options: Low probability: await ADAMTS13 activity before treating
High probability: start plasma exchange now, without waiting
Intermediate probability: give IVIG and repeat in 24 hours
Not valid with neurological signs: obtain MRI first
questions.explanation: A PLASMIC score of 6–7 indicates a high probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, and ADAMTS13 results often take days. The ISTH 2020 TTP guidelines support starting plasma exchange and corticosteroids when clinical suspicion is high, before confirmation; delaying plasma exchange beyond 24 h has been associated with higher mortality.

questions.q: Which initial treatment plan is most appropriate?
options: Daily plasma exchange and corticosteroids, plus rituximab
Platelet transfusion to above 50,000/µL, then plasma exchange
Eculizumab first; plasma exchange only if ADAMTS13 is low
IVIG and oral prednisone, then reassess the platelet count
questions.explanation: Plasma exchange removes the autoantibody and replaces ADAMTS13; corticosteroids are added, and the ISTH 2020 guidelines suggest rituximab (and caplacizumab) for immune TTP. Platelet transfusion is generally avoided unless bleeding is life-threatening, eculizumab is for complement-mediated HUS, and IVIG with prednisone treats ITP.

evidence.quote: A 24-year-old male presented to the emergency department (ED) with a chief complaint of headache and palpitations.
The patient ranked his headache, which had begun 7 days prior, as 6 out 10 on a pain scale and described it as sharp and constant.
He also reported 2–3 days of fatigue, palpitations, skin pallor, and gingival bleeding.
the patient's urine was dark reddish-brown, which he then reported had been similarly discolored for the past 7 days
his past medical history was unremarkable and without any family history of autoimmune disorders
He was afebrile, tachycardic (HR=119), and had a blood pressure of 131/68. His SpO² was 100% on room air with a respiratory rate of 18.
The physical exam revealed globalized pallor of his skin as well as conjunctival pallor.
Mucous membranes were found to be dry and pale with dried gingival hemorrhages apparent between teeth
Additionally, mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted.
Presenting initially as neurologically intact, the patient displayed a nonfocal lack of strength that resulted in a slow, but overall normal gait.
four hours after initial presentation to the ED, the patient developed difficulty with word-finding
He was otherwise neurologically intact, demonstrated by an ability to comprehend and repeat back in his own words what was conveyed to him.
a repeat head CT at this time of neurological change was unremarkable
blood urea nitrogen (BUN; 27mg/dL) and serum creatinine (1.4 mg/dL) levels were elevated, and his serum HCO2 was low (21mmol/L) with an anion gap of 14
hemoglobin (4.7 G/DL), hematocrit (14.2%), platelet count (10,000/mcl), and haptoglobin (<30 mg/dL) were all severely decreased
his LDH (1885 U/L) and indirect bilirubin (3.2 mg/dL) were significantly elevated
A peripheral blood smear (image) also revealed an abnormally high reticulocyte count (18.7%) and presence of schistocytes.
Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) was negative
prothrombin time (PT; 15.2 sec), partial thromboplastin time (PTT; 30.2 sec), and INR (1.2) were only slightly abnormal
A provisional diagnosis of TTP was made based on the clinical findings and PLASMIC score of 6.
The patient was admitted to the ICU and his serum was sent to an external laboratory for confirmation of insufficient ADAMTS13 activity.
therapeutic plasma exchange, several units of red blood cell transfusions, and immunosuppressive corticosteroids were initiated immediately
The following day, the patient had returned to his neurological baseline and no longer demonstrated word-finding difficulties.
His renal function also significantly improved during this time.
Results of the patient's serum sample showed an ADAMTS13 activity level less than 5% (normal =61% or higher) as well as antibodies against ADAMTS13.
He continued to receive daily plasmapheresis and prednisone.
On day three of ICU admission, there was a significant concern of relapse due to the continued presence of ADAMTS13 antibodies; therefore, the patient was administered rituximab.
On day six of admission, the patient's platelet levels normalized to 150,000/mcl.
After 10 days of admission, the patient was discharged as his hemoglobin and platelet levels remained stable off of plasmapheresis.
In total, he received ten rounds of plasmapheresis, five units of red blood cells, and one dose of rituximab, with the intention of three additional doses
discharged with instructions to continue taking pantoprazole (40mg/day) while tapering off of prednisone (60mg) over the following 24 days
His diminished ADAMTS13 activity level (<5%) and the presence of autoantibodies against ADAMTS13 confirmed a diagnosis of TTP.
